0.headline: Kalyan Krishnamurthy leaves Flipkart with its biggest battles still ahead
0.heading: Kalyan Krishnamurthy leaves Flipkart with its biggest battles still ahead
0.intro: Industry stakeholders say Krishnamurthy was an effective peacetime CEO who strengthened Flipkart's core business. His exit presents an opportunity for Walmart to take stock of the company's priorities and usher in a wartime leader to tackle intensifying competition, sharpen its portfolio and steer it towards profitability ahead of an eventual IPO
0.body:
Flipkart was arguably India's first new-age startup, spawning a generation of entrepreneurs from within its own ranks. Two decades later, many of those founders have taken their companies public, while Flipkart's own IPO remains elusive.

The company expanded into new categories and business segments while fending off competition. It retained its position as India's leading e-commerce player, but quick commerce has changed the landscape. Rivals that once focused on groceries are now delivering everything from electronics to iPhones in minutes, challenging Flipkart on its home turf.

The changing competitive landscape has also figured in discussions around Flipkart's delayed IPO, according to several current and former senior executives.

For Kalyan Krishnamurthy, who led Flipkart for more than 11 years, the task was to protect its e-commerce leadership while positioning the company for its next phase. He had a sizeable war chest and an established market position, but the challenges have grown.

"Kalyan was an exceptional peacetime CEO. He grew Flipkart's core business well and kept costs under control. However, he did not make bold enough bets and missed several key opportunities. Meesho scaled up in value commerce, Blinkit emerged as a leader in quick commerce, and Zudio made significant strides in offline retail. Flipkart entered some of these battles too late and failed to build meaningful consumer mindshare," said Tracxn co-founder and former Accel associate Abhishek Goyal.

Now Flipkart needs a wartime CEO, Goyal added.

More questions than answers

Krishnamurthy's exit comes at a critical juncture for the Walmart-owned company, which must balance a sprawling portfolio with the need to catch up in quick commerce and improve profitability.

Analysts see the transition as an opportunity for Walmart to reassess Flipkart's businesses, capital allocation and organisational structure. The incoming CEO will inherit a company competing across e-commerce, quick commerce, value commerce and fintech.

"One of the biggest criticisms of Flipkart has been that it has spread itself too thin and has not excelled in any one business," said an internet sector analyst.

Flipkart's bets on apparel, logistics and payments through Myntra, EKart Logistics and PhonePe have strengthened its market position. But social commerce platform Shopsy, travel company Cleartrip and pharmacy business SastaSundar have not delivered similar results. Its earlier quick-commerce bet, Flipkart Quick, was probably ahead of its time. The company continues to make new bets, including payments platform super.money.

Many of these newer businesses are deep in the red, while employees and investors are increasingly looking for returns on the time, effort and money invested.

Calls for a portfolio reset

Flipkart's focus on growth has also meant that profitability remains an important area for the company to address.

"Another key issue is that it has not focused enough on profitability. The company has been too focused on growth and is still operating with a 2005-2015 mindset of how to run startups and large companies in India. It has not adapted to profitability becoming a core metric," the analyst quoted above added.

The incoming CEO will have to bring sharper focus to the portfolio. Beyond its core e-commerce marketplace, Flipkart has pursued quick commerce through Minutes and is considering an entry into food delivery, putting it in competition with specialised players.

"The new management will have to distinguish between core and non-core businesses, concentrate capital on areas where Flipkart has a competitive advantage and reconsider investments that do not fit its longer-term strategy. This could involve shutting down some non-core operations, rationalising costs and potentially restructuring the group ahead of an IPO," said another analyst tracking the developments.

Flipkart will also have to decide whether to list the group as a whole or separate businesses such as Myntra and Cleartrip, analysts said.

Who takes the mantle?

A leadership change after more than a decade could bring fresh thinking as traditional e-commerce companies adapt to quick commerce.

"Sometimes, a change in leadership after 11 years can be a good thing for a company. The market has changed significantly, and it is no longer the same environment in which Flipkart began. Quick commerce has emerged as a major force, and even traditional e-commerce players are now adapting to that model," said Satish Meena, founder of e-commerce consultancy Datum Intelligence.

The incoming CEO will have to decide whether to pursue opportunities such as food delivery or strengthen existing businesses. The transition also follows a period of senior-level churn, with at least 14 vice-president and senior vice-president-level executives leaving over the past year or so, potentially influencing whether Walmart looks outside the company for a successor.

"The scale of the exits could make an external appointment more likely, particularly if Walmart wants a leader willing to challenge the company's existing strategy and take difficult decisions. An incoming CEO would also have to manage the risks of a sweeping organisational overhaul," said the second analyst quoted above.

Flipkart relies heavily on its people, and sharp headcount reductions or organisational changes could disrupt operations if not handled carefully, he said.

Closing the quick-commerce gap

Flipkart was an early mover in Indian e-commerce but was slower to respond as Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto built scale in instant deliveries. Its entry through Minutes came after the segment had become a major battleground.

It also faces competition from Meesho in value commerce and Amazon in the premium segment, while defending its presence in smaller cities.

"Flipkart has to reclaim the quick commerce space to stay relevant, and needs to build these hyperlocal capabilities rather than look at quick commerce and e-commerce as two entirely separate opportunities. That is an urgent priority. The fact that quick commerce scaled up right under Flipkart's nose could be one of the biggest misses of Kalyan's 11-year tenure," said Ankur Bisen, Senior Partner at The Knowledge Company.

The lingering IPO question

The leadership change could further delay Flipkart's IPO. Walmart had asked the company to defer its listing plans and prioritise operational profitability, with a target of reaching EBITDA breakeven before the end of FY27, Moneycontrol reported in May.

"A listing in 2028 would be aggressive. I don't see Flipkart going public before 2029. The new CEO will need time to settle in and make the changes required to prepare the company for a listing," one of the analysts quoted above said.

Datum's Meena said the incoming CEO would have to assess the company's financial position and prepare it for public-market scrutiny.

"Getting the company ready for a listing should be the top priority for whoever takes over. Everything else is secondary at this point," Meena said.

Rivals could sense an opportunity

The leadership transition could give competitors an opportunity to gain ground while Flipkart reviews its capital allocation and management priorities. Amazon, Meesho, Eternal and Swiggy are competing for different parts of the market that Flipkart wants to defend or expand in.

"While the leadership transition is underway, Flipkart's capital allocation decisions will be on hold. This could potentially disrupt its execution, giving rivals an opportunity to strengthen their position," one of the analysts quoted above said.

Flipkart must sharpen its portfolio and improve profitability without disrupting operations or ceding further ground to rivals. Its brand and scale remain significant advantages, but much will depend on whether Walmart gives the incoming CEO a clear mandate to address capability gaps and build a more convincing business for public-market investors.

1.headline: Mahanadi Coalfield shares to list tomorrow; analysts recommend trading strategy for Coal India unit
1.heading: Mahanadi Coalfield shares to list tomorrow; analysts recommend trading strategy for Coal India unit
1.intro: The stock suits long-term investors looking for steady dividends, while allottees who applied for listing gains can consider exiting, said an analyst.
1.body:
Shares of Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd. (MCL), a subsidiary of state-owned Coal India, are expected to make a flat debut on the exchanges on Friday, November 27, analysts said, advising investors with a long-term investment horizon to hold the shares.

However, investors seeking short-term gains may consider booking profits if the stock offers listing gains, they said.

Mahanadi Coalfields' Rs 8,981-crore initial public offering (IPO) was fully subscribed on the final day of bidding on November 23. The company had earlier raised Rs 2,295 crore from anchor investors. The price band for the issue was fixed at Rs 129-136 per share.

Mahesh M Ojha, VP Research and Business Development at Kantilal Chhaganlal Securities, said the long-term outlook for MCL remains positive, supported by its dominant position in coal production, substantial resource base and diversification opportunities.

"Long-term investors may consider holding the shares, while investors who receive IPO allotment with a short-term investment horizon may consider booking listing gains, if available," he said.

MCL is India's largest single coal-producing company and is primarily engaged in mining thermal-grade non-coking coal. It accounts for around 9.8 percent of the country's total coal resources, providing long-term visibility for its core business.

Ojha said the company plans to nearly triple its annual coal washery capacity to 37 million tonnes and diversify into coal gasification, renewable energy, mineral mining and rare earth elements.

It has also signed MoUs with the Odisha government for wind power and pumped energy storage projects and secured an 80 MW/320 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project.

At the upper price band of Rs 136, the issue is valued at around 8.4 times FY26 earnings and 5.9 times FY26 EV/EBITDA on post-issue capital, indicating a relatively fair valuation, he added.
Check All IPO News
Narendra Solanki, Head of Fundamental Research – Investment Services at Anand Rathi Shares and Stock Brokers, also expects the stock to list flat and advised investors to hold it from a long-term perspective.

MCL contributed 21 percent of India's domestic coal production in FY26. The company operates 17 mines across Odisha's Talcher and Ib Valley coalfields and has audited reserves of 9,840 million tonnes, providing an estimated mine life of 45 years.

Solanki said the company's mechanised opencast operations, rail connectivity and access to five ports support its logistics and low-cost operating structure.

The company also benefits from demand from power utilities and industrial customers, long-term fuel supply agreements and strong profitability. It reported an EBITDA margin of 41.7 percent and return on net worth (RoNW) of 53.8 percent in FY26.

Future growth is expected to be driven by mine expansion, increasing coal-washing capacity from 10 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) to 37 MTPA, first-mile connectivity projects and diversification into renewable energy and coal gasification, he said.

At the upper price band, MCL's valuation of 8.4 times FY26 price-to-earnings and 5.9 times FY26 EV/EBITDA is reasonable, Solanki added.

The proposed listing is part of Coal India's broader plan to unlock value from its subsidiaries through the capital markets. MCL is the third Coal India subsidiary to tap the public markets this year. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd was listed in January, while the IPO of Central Mine Planning &amp; Design Institute Ltd concluded in March.

Sarvam Goel, Founder of Pocketful, said the issue is entirely an offer for sale (OFS) by Coal India, meaning MCL will not receive any proceeds from it.

Excluding one-time income and tax credits in FY26, the issue is priced at around nine times earnings, representing a premium of nearly 30 percent to Coal India, he said.

"We expect a flat listing over the Rs 90,010 crore market cap. The stock suits long-term investors looking for steady dividends, while allottees who applied for listing gains can consider exiting," Goel added.

2.headline: End of the grey market scoreboard – Will retail investors simply switch to another one?
2.heading: End of the grey market scoreboard – Will retail investors simply switch to another one?
2.intro: Retail participants will simply swap one signal for a better one. In essence, the retail investor will continue with a herd mentality rather than taking the pains to understand the company they are investing in
2.body:
Highlights

 	SEBI bans GMP publication
 	SEBI calls GMPs unregulated and says publishing them may harm investors
 	Investors betting on GMP cannot use the ODR portal for related disputes
 	Retail investors will turn to official oversubscription data, continuing their herd mentality

SEBI on Monday advised all registered intermediaries and market participants to stop publishing grey market premium (GMP) figures for upcoming IPOs. The advisory covers publication, display, circulation and dissemination across every mode and platform, including websites, email, SMS and social media.

The regulator correctly described these pre-listing premiums as unofficial, unverified and unregulated, and said that publishing them may harm investors and run against the principles of transparency and accountability in the securities market.

However, for those investors who still bet on unauthorised GMP, it reminded them that grievance redressal mechanisms, including the ODR portal, would not be available for any dispute arising from such transactions.

Before commenting on SEBI’s action, let’s look at what the grey market premium actually is. When an IPO opens for subscription, a parallel and informal market gets activated. Dealers and operators quote a price at which the shares would trade even before they list. The gap between that quote and the IPO price becomes the premium. A premium of Rs 100 on an issue priced at Rs 400 suggests the stock could list at Rs 500. Websites, YouTube channels and media carry these numbers, and many retail investors treat them as a forecast of listing day gains.

SEBI's action was long overdue, as there was no transparency over how GMP numbers came to exist. They were never produced through any scientific process. There was no stated methodology, no audit trail and no standard way of arriving at a figure. A number would appear on a website in the morning and change by evening, and nobody could say where it was generated from.

SEBI noted that the figures were widely published across websites, digital platforms and newspapers, and even by some registered intermediaries, often as indicators of likely listing prices.

The grey market is not controlled by the regulator. There were no official transactions of shares based on these numbers, though unofficially, and in bucket shops, these numbers were given prominence.

For a retail investor, especially one investing for the listing pop, GMP was an important number. A higher number could draw in more applications, and a lower one could shake out nervous holders.

Eshaan Lazarus, founder and CEO of 021 Trade, backs the regulator's move. "I believe SEBI is correct to ask intermediaries not to publish such numbers. These numbers are unregulated estimates at best, and pump-and-dump schemes at worst, and investors should not rely on them to make decisions."

Even so, the number had its utility in the short term. For a retail trader deciding whether to bid in an IPO that closed in few days, GMP offered a free and instant sentiment gauge.

Many traders used it to decide how much to apply for based on the premium. A strong GMP never guaranteed a gain, and plenty of issues with hefty premiums listed flat or below the issue price.

So, what happens when the scoreboard goes dark?

Not much, the scoreboard will change.

SEBI's research has shown that nearly two-thirds of investors exit a stock within a week of its listing. Just stopping the GMP numbers will not make them long-term investors. Instead, these players will look at the oversubscription data that the exchanges publish through the bidding window.

Subscription by category is official and updated through the day by the exchanges. It shows how many times the retail portion is covered and how aggressively various players are bidding, especially institutional buyers.

An issue with strong institutional participation attracts retail investors, as the general perception is that institutional players would have done their research before investing. The same is true of anchor investors, who invest in the company before the IPO. Marquee anchor investors bring more retail investors to a company's issue.

Retail participants will simply swap one signal for a better one. In essence, the retail investor will continue with a herd mentality rather than taking the pains to understand the company they are investing in.

We will continue to see investors exiting stocks that have listed at a premium within the first week. An issue that is heavily oversubscribed, with a limited free float and eager buyers, can spike on day one. A weak book can drag a good company below its issue price for a few sessions.

Neither outcome tells you much about the company itself. Warren Buffett correctly explained the situation when he said that in the short run the market is a voting machine, but in the long run it is a weighing machine.

Grey market premiums were a way of counting votes before the election had even begun. SEBI's advisory removes one tally, but the voting will carry on through subscription data and listing-day trading.
